scope.start: 12a: Mishnah: the animals that may not redeem a firstborn donkey
scope.end: 12b: Rav Mari's 'like the gazelle and like the hart' applied to R. Shimon as well

sections.title: Mishnah: Only a Lamb Redeems; R. Eliezer on the Hybrid and Koy
sections.gist: The first tanna rules out six kinds of animal for redeeming a *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey). R. Eliezer accepts a sheep–goat hybrid but not a *koy*, and a kohen given the donkey itself must first redeem it.

bullets.text: First tanna: a *peter chamor* may not be redeemed with a calf, a wild animal, a slaughtered animal, a *tereifah*, a hybrid of sheep and goat, or a *koy* (an animal whose status, domestic or wild, is in doubt).
R. Eliezer: a hybrid of sheep and goat is permitted, because it counts as a lamb. A *koy* is forbidden, because its status is in doubt.
If the owner gave the *peter chamor* itself to a kohen, the kohen may not keep it until he designates a lamb in its place.

illustration.caption: The Mishnah's list, in its order, of animals that may not redeem a *peter chamor* in place of the lamb the verse requires. R. Eliezer differs only on the sheep–goat hybrid (Bekhorot 12a).

sections.title: The Source: Lamb–Lamb from the Paschal Offering, and 'You Shall Redeem' Twice
sections.gist: The first clause is ben Bag Bag's: a *gezeirah shavah* to the Paschal offering excludes the Mishnah's animals, while the doubled 'you shall redeem' keeps female, blemished and older lambs valid.

bullets.text: The first clause follows ben Bag Bag. "Lamb" for the *peter chamor* (Shemot 13:13) and "lamb" for the Paschal offering (Shemot 12:3) form a *gezeirah shavah*: every animal excluded from the Paschal offering is excluded here too.
Challenge: then the redemption lamb should also be male, unblemished and in its first year, like the Paschal offering.
Answer: "you shall redeem" is written twice (Shemot 13:13, 34:20). The repetition includes female lambs, blemished lambs and lambs past their first year.
Challenge: then let the repetition include the Mishnah's animals as well. Answer: if so, the lamb–lamb analogy would serve no purpose.

chart.caption: What each derivation does to the redemption lamb
rows: Calf, wild animal, slaughtered animal, *tereifah*, hybrid, *koy*
Excluded, as from the Paschal offering
Lambs that are female, blemished or past their first year

sections.title: Borderline Lambs: Ben Pekua, Nidmeh, Pesulei Ha'mukdashin
sections.gist: Three questions on animals at the edge of the rule: a *ben pekua*, a lamb that looks like another species (*nidmeh*), and redeemed *pesulei ha'mukdashin*.
sections.continues: Continues on 12b: the next question, whether a *peter chamor* may be redeemed with an animal bought with *Shevi'it* produce.

children.title: Ben Pekua: Slaughtered Meat or a Walking Lamb?
children.gist: The question arises only on the Rabbis' view; Mar Zutra forbids a *ben pekua* and Rav Ashi permits it, arguing over the same two derivations as before.

children.title: Why the Question Arises Only for the Rabbis
children.gist: For R. Meir a *ben pekua* needs its own slaughter and is a full lamb; for the Rabbis its mother's slaughter permits it, so is it slaughtered meat or a living lamb?

bullets.text: The question: may a *peter chamor* be redeemed with a *ben pekua*, a lamb taken out alive from its slaughtered mother?
Not according to R. Meir: he requires the *ben pekua* to be slaughtered itself, so it is a full-fledged lamb.
According to the Rabbis, its mother's slaughter already permits it. Is it like meat in a pot, and so a slaughtered animal the Mishnah excludes? Or, since it walks around now, is it called a lamb?

illustration.caption: The two ways the Gemara frames a *ben pekua* on the Rabbis' view, with the rulings of Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi beneath (Bekhorot 12a).

children.title: Mar Zutra vs. Rav Ashi: Does 'You Shall Redeem' Include It?
children.gist: Mar Zutra forbids and Rav Ashi permits; their exchange replays the Gemara's earlier back-and-forth over the Paschal analogy and the doubled verb.

bullets.text: Mar Zutra: one may not redeem a *peter chamor* with a *ben pekua*. Rav Ashi: one may.
Rav Ashi: if your reason is that you learn from the Paschal offering, for which a *ben pekua* is unfit, then require a male, unblemished, first-year lamb as well.
Mar Zutra: the doubled "you shall redeem" includes lambs that are not male, unblemished or in their first year.
Rav Ashi: then it includes a *ben pekua* too. Mar Zutra: if so, what is the lamb–lamb analogy for? The Gemara leaves the dispute there.

chart.caption: Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi on redeeming with a *ben pekua*
rows: The lamb–lamb analogy excludes what the Paschal offering excludes; the doubled 'you shall redeem' adds only female, blemished and older lambs
If the doubled verb includes a *ben pekua*, the analogy has no purpose
The doubled 'you shall redeem' includes a *ben pekua*, just as it includes female, blemished and older lambs
If you learn from the Paschal offering, require a male, unblemished, first-year lamb too

returns_to.note: The same exchange over the lamb–lamb analogy and the doubled verb

children.title: Nidmeh: Do the Rabbis Accept a Look-Alike Lamb?
children.gist: Whether the Rabbis, who reject a hybrid, still accept a lamb that looks like a goat: two baraitot are brought as proofs, and both are deflected.

children.title: The Question: Hybrid Excluded, but a Nidmeh?
children.gist: R. Eliezer surely accepts a *nidmeh*, since he accepts even a hybrid; the question is whether the Rabbis distinguish the two.

bullets.text: The question: may a *peter chamor* be redeemed with a *nidmeh*, a lamb born of two sheep that looks like another species, such as a goat?
Not according to R. Eliezer: he accepts even a hybrid of sheep and goat, so certainly a *nidmeh*.
According to the Rabbis, who reject a hybrid: do they accept a *nidmeh*, or is there no difference between them?

children.title: A Cow's Goat-Like Offspring: Follow the Mother
children.gist: A baraita forbids the goat-like offspring of a cow, implying that a ewe's is permitted; the Gemara assigns it to R. Eliezer, teaching that the mother decides.

bullets.text: Baraita: if a cow gave birth to a goat of sorts, one may not redeem a *peter chamor* with it. Inference: if a ewe gave birth to a goat of sorts, one may.
That can't be R. Eliezer, who accepts even a hybrid; so it must be the Rabbis, and they accept a *nidmeh*.
Deflection: it is R. Eliezer's view, and it teaches the cow's case itself. Don't follow the offspring's appearance and call it a goat; follow its mother, and it is a calf, which cannot redeem.

illustration.caption: The baraita's case, read as R. Eliezer's: a cow's goat-like offspring follows its mother and counts as a calf. A ewe's goat-like offspring is the *nidmeh* whose status for the Rabbis stays open (Bekhorot 12a).

children.title: Rabba bar Shmuel's Baraita: Offerings, Firstborn, Tithe or Redemption?
children.gist: A *nidmeh* is treated like a hybrid, but for which law? Offerings and firstborn status have their own verses, and the Gemara finds the baraita a role in animal tithe, so it proves nothing about redemption.

bullets.text: Rabba bar Shmuel's baraita: a hybrid is a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts whose father is a lamb.
With a lamb for a father, that is no hybrid but a *nidmeh*. So read: this is the animal that resembles a hybrid, which the Rabbis treated like one.
Offerings? That needs no baraita: in Vayikra 22:27, "a bull, or a lamb" excludes a hybrid, and "or a goat" excludes a *nidmeh*.
Firstborn status? Also no need: "the firstborn of an ox" (Bamidbar 18:17) means an ox whose firstborn is an ox.
Animal tithe? Also no need: "under" (Vayikra 22:27, offerings) and "under" (Vayikra 27:32, tithe) form a *gezeirah shavah*.
So, the proof argues, the baraita must mean the redemption lamb: a *nidmeh* cannot redeem a *peter chamor*.

Deflection: it is about animal tithe, for a *nidmeh* with some features of its mother. Such an animal does have firstborn status, and "passing" (tithe) and "passing" (firstborn) might have extended that to tithe; the baraita teaches that the "under"/"under" analogy governs, so it is excluded.
So the baraita proves nothing about redeeming a *peter chamor*.

chart.caption: Where a *nidmeh* is already excluded, and what that leaves for the baraita
rows: Yes, for a *nidmeh* with some features of its mother, lest "passing" / "passing" link it to firstborn status
The proof's reading, set aside once the tithe role is found

children.title: Redeemed Pesulei Ha'mukdashin: Transfer or Removal, and the Gazelle and Hart
children.gist: Whether an animal already under its own prohibitions can redeem: the question turns on *ein issur chal al issur*, and Rav Mari settles it from 'like the gazelle and like the hart', for R. Shimon too.

children.title: Does Redemption Transfer the Prohibition to the Lamb?
children.gist: Only R. Yehuda, who forbids benefit from a *peter chamor*, raises the question: if redemption moves the prohibition onto the lamb, *ein issur chal al issur* blocks it; if it only lifts the prohibition, nothing does.

bullets.text: The question: may a *peter chamor* be redeemed with *pesulei ha'mukdashin* that were redeemed, which may still not be shorn or worked? Does *ein issur chal al issur* apply here?
Not according to R. Shimon: he permits benefit from a *peter chamor*, so it is non-sacred and no prohibition passes to the lamb.
According to R. Yehuda, who forbids benefit from it: perhaps the donkey's prohibition must be able to pass to the lamb, and it cannot take hold on an animal already forbidden.
Or perhaps, since the lamb itself stays permitted, redemption only removes the donkey's prohibition, and the principle does not come into play.

chart.caption: The two sides of the question, on R. Yehuda's view
rows: Moves the donkey's prohibition onto the lamb
Applies: the lamb is already forbidden
Only lifts the donkey's prohibition; the lamb stays permitted

children.title: Rav Mari: 'Like the Gazelle and Like the Hart', Even for R. Shimon
children.gist: Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana: the Torah likens *pesulei ha'mukdashin* to a gazelle and a hart, which cannot redeem, so neither can they; on this basis they fail for R. Shimon as well.

bullets.text: Rav Mari son of Rav Kahana: the Torah says *pesulei ha'mukdashin* are "like the gazelle and like the hart" (Devarim 12:15). A gazelle or hart cannot redeem a *peter chamor*, so neither can they.
The Gemara adds: once this is the reason, *pesulei ha'mukdashin* cannot redeem according to R. Shimon either, since the same verse applies to them.

illustration.caption: Rav Mari's answer: the Torah likens redeemed *pesulei ha'mukdashin* to a gazelle and a hart, and neither of those can redeem a *peter chamor* (Devarim 12:15, on Bekhorot 12a–12b).

returns_to.note: Returns to R. Shimon, whom the question had set aside

key_terms.sense: the firstborn donkey that must be redeemed
key_terms.definition: The firstborn male of a donkey, which its owner must redeem with a lamb given to a kohen; if he does not redeem it, he breaks its neck.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks which animals may serve as the redemption lamb, and which borderline lambs qualify.

key_terms.definition: A rule of Torah interpretation that links two passages sharing a word or phrase, so that laws stated in one apply to the other.
key_terms.on_this_daf: "Lamb"/"lamb" ties the redemption lamb to the Paschal offering, and "under"/"under" and "passing"/"passing" are weighed for animal tithe.

key_terms.sense: fetus found alive in a slaughtered animal
key_terms.definition: A live young taken from the womb of an animal that was ritually slaughtered. According to the Rabbis the mother's slaughter permits it to be eaten; R. Meir requires it to be slaughtered itself.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether it counts as slaughtered meat or as a lamb for redeeming a firstborn donkey: Mar Zutra forbids, Rav Ashi permits.

key_terms.sense: hybrid of a sheep and a goat
key_terms.definition: An animal born of two different species, such as a sheep and a goat, which halakha treats as distinct from either parent species in many areas.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The first tanna forbids redeeming a firstborn donkey with a sheep–goat hybrid, while R. Eliezer permits it because it counts as a lamb.

key_terms.definition: An animal born of parents of one species that looks like an animal of a different species, such as a lamb born of sheep that resembles a goat.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether the Rabbis, who reject a hybrid, accept a *nidmeh* for redemption; both proofs brought are deflected.

key_terms.sense: blemished consecrated animals that were redeemed
key_terms.definition: Consecrated animals disqualified from the altar, usually by a blemish, and redeemed. They may be slaughtered and eaten but may still not be shorn or worked.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether they can redeem a firstborn donkey; Rav Mari rules them out because the Torah likens them to a gazelle and a hart.

key_terms.sense: a prohibition cannot take hold where one already exists
key_terms.definition: The principle that a new prohibition does not take effect on an object or act that is already forbidden by an existing prohibition.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It would block redeeming with *pesulei ha'mukdashin* only if redemption moves the donkey's prohibition onto the lamb, rather than merely lifting it.

judgment_calls: The three questions (ben pekua, nidmeh, pesulei ha'mukdashin) are grouped under one parent, 'Borderline Lambs', since all ask whether an edge-case animal can serve as the redemption lamb; each could instead be its own top-level section. Grouping lets the parent's gist and 'continues' show that the series goes on into 12b.
ben Bag Bag's derivation (s2) is its own top-level section rather than a child of the Mishnah, because it sets up the two derivations that the later questions (especially ben pekua) return to.

The ben pekua question is split into its framing (R. Meir vs. the Rabbis, meat in a pot vs. a walking lamb) and the Mar Zutra–Rav Ashi dispute; it could be a single flat section. It is split because the framing and the dispute rest on different arguments.

The Gemara's closing extension to R. Shimon (12a.25–12b.1) is kept with Rav Mari's answer in one section, with a returns_to link to the framing that had set R. Shimon aside, rather than made its own section.
coverage_notes: No shiur for this daf; the whole outline is built from the Gemara text.
The previous daf's essay tail covers only 11b (terumat ma'aser and the lamb that died), all outside this scope.
The Mishnah's last clause (a kohen given the donkey must first redeem it) is discussed in the Gemara at 12b.14, beyond this outline's end; here it appears only as a Mishnah bullet.
The series of questions continues at 12b.2 with an animal bought with Shevi'it produce, outside this scope.
